solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Home, well-behaved? Something believed sincerely

parts.note: to be in is to be at home
a well-behaved child is good
a faith is something believed

explanation.surface: Someone checks that home life is orderly and that their beliefs are sincerely held.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is only the last word; 'Something believed sincerely' reads as one phrase, but 'sincerely' breaks off to define the whole answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Acting in good faith means acting honestly and sincerely.

clue.text: Expecting popular pupils? Half missing!

parts.note: what is in is popular
PUPILS with its second half (ILS) gone

explanation.surface: A teacher expecting a crowded classroom finds half the pupils absent.
explanation.walkthrough: IN PUP is said of a pregnant dog, so 'Expecting' is a fair definition even though the surface is about a school.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom for a pregnant dog, and 'expecting' is the everyday euphemism for pregnant.

clue.text: Expert in soil — go get changed

indicators.note: the letters are changed into a new order

parts.note: anagram fodder, used again from the definition
anagram fodder

explanation.surface: Someone is told to fetch the soil expert and get changed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Soil' does double duty: it finishes the definition and also supplies four letters of the fodder, which 'go get' alone cannot fill.
explanation.definitionFit: A geologist studies rocks and soils.

clue.text: Working in relation to tax

definitions.meaning: the first sense: at one's post, as a nurse on a shift is
ON = about, DUTY = a tax, as on imported goods

explanation.surface: A line from a tax office: working on matters of tax.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense reads the phrase literally: 'on' as in 'a talk on', and a duty is a tax.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom for being at one's post, as a nurse or guard is; read literally it is a phrase about a levy on goods.

clue.text: As you say, gosh, not many here!

indicators.note: the letters come from how the word is spoken

parts.note: phew is an exclamation like gosh

explanation.surface: Someone surveys an almost empty room and exclaims how few people came.
explanation.walkthrough: PHEW and FEW sound the same; the exclamation mark belongs to the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a small number, as in 'a handful turned up'.

clue.text: Initially irritated, rising uproar about drink, tasteless

indicators.note: initially means only the opening letter of irritated is used

parts.note: first letter of irritated

indicators.note: about means the reversed word goes around the other piece
in a down clue, rising means the word is read upwards, so backwards

parts.note: a din is a loud uproar
to sip is to drink, and a sip is a small drink

explanation.surface: Someone annoyed by a noisy row over drinks, finding it all rather dull.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rising' turns DIN upwards to NID, and 'about' wraps that around SIP, giving NSIPID after the opening I.
explanation.definitionFit: Insipid food or drink lacks flavour, so it is a synonym for bland and tasteless.

clue.text: New court rule hit garden business

indicators.note: the letters form a new arrangement

parts.note: anagram fodder, 12 letters

explanation.surface: A new court ruling has hurt the garden centre trade.
explanation.walkthrough: The legal surface hides that all twelve letters are there to be rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: The science and trade of growing plants, fruit and flowers, which is what nurseries and garden centres live by.

clue.text: Bold porter regularly displaying extravagance

indicators.note: take letters at regular intervals: every other one

parts.note: P, R and E: the first, third and fifth letters of porter
something sumptuous is lavish, displaying extravagance

explanation.surface: A cheeky hotel porter shows off expensive tastes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bold' here means cheeky or forward, not brave.
explanation.definitionFit: Presumptuous behaviour is overbold, taking liberties.

clue.text: Feature of parachute drop starts to cause regular injuries unfortunately

indicators.note: unfortunately suggests things going wrong, so these letters end up jumbled
starts to means the opening letters of the following words are taken

parts.note: first letters of cause, regular, injuries

explanation.surface: A parachute drop that leads to frequent injuries when things go badly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'starts to' gives CRI, the first letters of cause, regular and injuries; these join DROP and 'unfortunately' shuffles the lot.
explanation.definitionFit: A ripcord is the cord pulled to open a parachute, so it is one part of the equipment.

clue.text: Wife is extremely eager, extra shrewd

indicators.note: extremely means only the outermost letters of eager are used

parts.note: first and last letters of eager

explanation.surface: A wife who is keen and unusually astute.
explanation.walkthrough: 'extremely' takes the two ends of eager, E and R.
explanation.definitionFit: Wiser is the comparative of wise, meaning more shrewd or sensible than someone else.

clue.text: Was a fan of fantastic Reds up top

indicators.note: the letters are fantastically rearranged

parts.note: anagram fodder, 9 letters

explanation.surface: A football fan used to follow a brilliant Reds side at the top of the league.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reds' suggests a football team (Liverpool or Manchester United), which is the scene: the answer is what a fan did.
explanation.definitionFit: The British sporting sense: a fan follows and backs a club, and the past tense matches 'Was'.

clue.text: Small drink at first for writer

parts.note: a dram is a small measure of whisky
used as written
1ST, with the 1 written as I

explanation.surface: A writer has a small drink first thing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At first' looks like one phrase meaning initially, but it splits: AT, then 1ST with the numeral as I.
explanation.definitionFit: A playwright is one particular kind of writer, so the definition is a broad category.

clue.text: Greek character's quiet greeting

parts.note: p = piano, quietly in music
hi is a greeting

explanation.surface: A Greek person gives a soft hello.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Character' means a letter of the alphabet, not a person; the ’s stands for 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: A character is a letter, and this is the 21st letter of the Greek alphabet.

clue.text: Believer's arithmetic calculation recalled little interesting maths to begin with

definitions.note: Believer's reads as 'believer is', the definition plus a link

indicators.note: recalled means called back, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: a sum is an arithmetic calculation

indicators.note: to begin with means the first letters of the following words are taken

parts.note: first letters of little, interesting, maths

explanation.surface: A believer remembers a sum, with a bit of interesting maths at the start.
explanation.walkthrough: 'recalled' turns SUM into MUS, and 'to begin with' takes LIM from little, interesting, maths.
explanation.definitionFit: A Muslim is a follower of Islam, so one kind of religious believer.

clue.text: Newspaper pay increase — everyday event?

parts.note: The Sun is a British tabloid newspaper
in Britain a pay rise is a raise

explanation.surface: A newspaper's staff get a pay rise, and wonder whether that will happen every day.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that 'everyday event' is a playful definition: the sun rises every single day.
explanation.definitionFit: Sunrise happens every morning.

clue.text: Secure gold in vehicle

parts.note: to land a deal is to secure it
Au is the chemical symbol for gold

explanation.surface: Someone locks up gold inside a vehicle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like a container instruction, but here it only links definition to wordplay; a landau is an old horse-drawn carriage.
explanation.definitionFit: A landau is a four-wheeled horse-drawn carriage with a folding top.

clue.text: Leaves Selby carrying vase maybe

indicators.note: the phrase carries the answer inside it

parts.note: leaVES SELby

explanation.surface: Someone leaves the Yorkshire town of Selby carrying a vase.
explanation.walkthrough: Selby is a town in North Yorkshire; 'maybe' marks a vase as one example of the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A vase is a kind of vessel, a container for liquid.

clue.text: Money, two notes

parts.note: the first note: TI, the seventh note of the sol-fa scale (do re mi)
the second note: n., the abbreviation for note, as in a footnote

explanation.surface: A payment made in two banknotes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Notes' looks like banknotes, but one is a note of the scale and the other the abbreviation n. for note; tin is old British slang for money.
explanation.definitionFit: Tin is dated British slang for money.

clue.text: Believer in God accepts blame for counsellor

indicators.note: one word takes the other in

parts.note: a theist believes in God
to take the rap is to take the blame; it goes inside THE…IST

explanation.surface: A religious believer takes the blame on behalf of a counsellor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Believer in God accepts blame' reads like a confession, but 'accepts' is the container, and the thing taken in is a slang word: to take the rap.
explanation.definitionFit: Near synonyms: both are professionals who help clients by talking through their problems.

clue.text: Island fellow penning one poem

parts.note: I = island, as on maps

indicators.note: the fellow pens, or encloses, the one

parts.note: a lad is a fellow
I is the Roman numeral one; it goes inside L…AD

explanation.surface: A man on an island writes a single poem.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Penning' suggests writing, which suits a poem, but here it means enclosing.
explanation.definitionFit: The Iliad is Homer's epic poem of the Trojan War.

clue.text: Nothing held back wicked girl

indicators.note: the word is held backwards

parts.note: EVIL (wicked) written backwards
O looks like zero

explanation.surface: A wicked girl holds nothing back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nothing held back' reads as a phrase meaning total candour, but the reversal applies to 'wicked'.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: crosswords often define a first name just as 'girl' or 'boy', and this is a traditional English girl's name.

clue.text: Untrustworthy person in shelter after revolution

indicators.note: the word has turned round

parts.note: the lee is the sheltered side, away from the wind; this word is then turned round

explanation.surface: A traitor hides out in a shelter after a political revolution.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolution' looks political, and it means a turning round.
explanation.definitionFit: A figurative sense: the fish is so slippery to hold that its name is used for an evasive, shifty person.

clue.text: NE Irish broadcast shedding more light?

indicators.note: the letters are scattered about

parts.note: anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A radio programme from the north-east of Ireland explains more about a topic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shedding more light' reads as explaining, and the question mark admits the literal sense: glowing brighter.
explanation.definitionFit: A literal reading of an idiom: a brighter, glossier surface throws off more light, while 'shedding light' usually means explaining.

clue.text: Providing strong protection lest pet deal unravels

indicators.note: the letters come apart and are rewoven

parts.note: anagram fodder, 11 letters

explanation.surface: An owner wants sturdy protection in case a deal over a pet falls apart.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is descriptive: armour of steel plates gives strong protection.
explanation.definitionFit: A descriptive definition: armour of hard metal sheets is what gives warships and vaults strong protection.
